Topic 01 — General Aspects of New Facility Design

Four Phases

Every new facility build moves through four sequential phases — skipping one costs far more later.

1
Predesign
2
Design
3
Construction
4

Photo by Pedro Miranda on Unsplash
Topic 01 — General Aspects of New Facility Design · 1 of 4

Predesign — Before Ground Breaks

What It Is
Earliest phase — needs assessment, budget, and site selection before any drawings exist.
Design committee formed: S&C staff, athletic administration, architect, sports medicine.
How It Works
Feasibility study → confirms budget matches program needs before committing.
S&C professional's input here is critical — decisions made now are the hardest to reverse later.
Training Implication
A coach absent from predesign inherits a ceiling too low for the platform or a floor plan with no sightlines — get a seat at this table early.
Photo by Soham Banerjee on Unsplash
Topic 01 — General Aspects of New Facility Design · 2 of 4

Design — Drawings Take Shape

What It Is
Predesign needs → architectural schematics, blueprints, and equipment layout drawings.
How It Works
Iterative stakeholder review — S&C staff check sightlines, spacing, and traffic flow on paper before construction locks them in.
Training Implication
Mark up the blueprint with actual platform footprints and rack clearances — architects size rooms, not squat racks.
Photo by Mohd Syahril Khalid on Unsplash
Topic 01 — General Aspects of New Facility Design · 3 of 4

Construction — Building It Out

What It Is
Contractor bids awarded → physical build begins per approved design-phase drawings.
How It Works
Scheduled inspections at each stage (electrical, HVAC, flooring) → change orders reviewed against original design intent.
Training Implication
Walk the site during rough-in — an outlet or drain moved 3 feet is a paper change now, a jackhammer later.
Photo by Ambitious Studio* | Rick Barrett on Unsplash
Topic 01 — General Aspects of New Facility Design · 4 of 4

Preoperation — Ready to Open

What It Is
Final phase before doors open — staff hiring, equipment purchase/installation, policy writing.
How It Works
Soft-opening walkthrough → test equipment, supervision sightlines, and emergency procedures before athletes arrive.
Training Implication
Policies (facility rules, emergency action plan) must exist before session one — not drafted reactively after an incident.

Topic 02 — Existing, Satellite, and Outdoor Training Facilities

Three Facility Types

Not every S&C facility gets built from scratch — each type carries its own constraints.

1
Existing Facility
2
Satellite Facility
3
Outdoor Training Facility
Photo by Mike Cox on Unsplash
Topic 02 — Existing, Satellite, and Outdoor Facilities · 1 of 3

Existing Facility — Working Within Fixed Bones

What It Is
Renovation of a pre-existing space rather than new construction — structure already fixed.
How It Works
Constraints: support columns, ceiling height, existing electrical/plumbing runs limit layout options.
Training Implication
Audit structural constraints before buying equipment — a platform doesn't fit around a load-bearing column.
Photo by Ambitious Studio* | Rick Barrett on Unsplash
Topic 02 — Existing, Satellite, and Outdoor Facilities · 2 of 3

Satellite Facility — Extending Reach

What It Is
Smaller, off-site or auxiliary training space serving a specific team or location.
How It Works
Scaled-down equipment set matched to the sports it serves; supervision protocols mirror the main facility.
Training Implication
Standardize policy and equipment specs across satellites — athletes shouldn't get a different safety standard off-site.
Photo by Gabin Vallet on Unsplash
Topic 02 — Existing, Satellite, and Outdoor Facilities · 3 of 3

Outdoor Training Facility — Exposed to the Elements

What It Is
Turf fields, tracks, and open-air training spaces used for speed, agility, and conditioning work.
How It Works
Weather drives scheduling and equipment durability; dedicated storage needed for sleds, cones, and portable equipment.
Training Implication
Build a weather contingency plan (heat, lightning, surface condition) into the facility's standard operating procedures.
Topic 03

Assessing Athletic
Program Needs

Photo by Sum Sum on Unsplash
Topic 03 — Assessing Athletic Program Needs

What Drives the Assessment

  • Athletes Number of athletes & teams served → sets total floor space and equipment count
  • Sports Sports offered → determines specialty equipment (platforms, turf, throwing areas)
  • Usage Peak usage times → multiple teams training simultaneously drives capacity planning
  • Growth Projected program growth → build in expansion room, not just current headcount
  • Stakeholders Coach, administration & sports-medicine input → each has different space priorities
  • Budget Available budget → sets the ceiling on space, equipment, and finish quality
Topic 03 — Assessing Athletic Program Needs

Turning Needs Into Space

Space Allocation
Rule-of-thumb square footage per athlete, scaled by peak simultaneous users, not average.
Priority Setting
Needs analysis ranks must-have vs. nice-to-have space → protects core training area if budget shrinks.
100 SQ FT
(9.3 m²) minimum per individual — athletes, staff & coaches combined
100 FT·LB/FT²
(4.8 kN/m²) minimum floor load-bearing capacity
Size for the busiest hour of the week, not the average — that's when supervision and safety margins get tested.

Topic 04 — Facility Location, Access, and Structural Considerations

Four Structural Factors

Where the facility sits and how it's built determines whether it's safe to supervise and safe to train in.

1
Supervision Location
2
Access
3
Ceiling Height
4
Flooring
Topic 04 — Location, Access & Structural Considerations · 1 of 4

Supervision Location — Seeing Everything

What It Is
Placement that gives staff an unobstructed sightline across the entire training floor.
How It Works
Elevated office/control point, or a central open-floor position → one glance covers every area.
Training Implication
A blind corner is where an injury goes unnoticed — design layout around supervision, not around it.
Photo: Pixabay
Topic 04 — Location, Access & Structural Considerations · 2 of 4

Access — Controlling Entry

What It Is
Single, controlled point of entry/exit for security, sign-in, and supervision.
How It Works
ADA-compliant routes throughout — any height change over 0.5 in. (1.3 cm) needs a ramp (12 in. run per 1 in. rise) or lift.
Training Implication
Multiple unsupervised entrances defeat the emergency action plan — one door, one accountability point.
Topic 04 — Location, Access & Structural Considerations · 3 of 4

Ceiling Height — Clearing the Bar

What It Is
Minimum vertical clearance for overhead bar path & jumps: 12 to 14 ft (3.7–4.3 m) recommended.
How It Works
12 ft (3.7 m) minimum for a jerk overhead + plate clearance; higher still for banner/rig-mounted equipment.
Training Implication
A low ceiling silently rules out Olympic lifting variations for taller athletes — measure before the platform ships.
Photo by Ambitious Studio* | Rick Barrett on Unsplash
Topic 04 — Location, Access & Structural Considerations · 4 of 4

Flooring — Matching Surface to Load

What It Is
Surface selection driven by what's dropped, dragged, or run on it in each zone.
How It Works
Rubber flooring under platforms/free weights absorbs dropped-bar impact; turf for sled work; resilient flooring elsewhere.
Training Implication
The wrong floor under a platform transmits impact to the slab below → structural damage and noise complaints from neighboring rooms.
Topic 04 — Location, Access & Structural Considerations

Numbers You Must Know

FactorFigure
Height change that requires a ramp or lift0.5 in (1.3 cm)
Ramp ratio (run : rise)12:1
Ceiling height — recommended12–14 ft (3.7–4.3 m)
Ceiling height — absolute minimum12 ft (3.7 m)
Floor load-bearing capacity — minimum100 ft·lb/ft² (4.8 kN/m²)

Topic 05 — Environmental and Support Systems

Four Support Systems

The systems athletes never notice when they're right — and can't miss when they're wrong.

1
Lighting
2
Temp / Humidity / Ventilation
3
Sound
4
Electrical Service
Photo by Ambitious Studio* | Rick Barrett on Unsplash
Topic 05 — Environmental and Support Systems · 1 of 4

Lighting — Seeing the Lift

What It Is
20–30 fc (200–300 lux) at floor level for general areas, up to 50 fc (500 lux) for resistance/group zones.
How It Works
LED at 4,000–5,000K reads as daylight; combine with natural light where possible and avoid glare on mirrors/screens.
Training Implication
Poor lighting hides technique breakdown a coach needs to see — under-lit platforms are a coaching blind spot.
Topic 05 — Environmental and Support Systems · 2 of 4

Temperature, Humidity & Ventilation

What It Is
68–78°F (20–26°C) is the appropriate range — optimal is 68–74°F (20–23°C); humidity ≤60%.
How It Works
HVAC sized for peak occupancy, not empty-room conditions; air exchanged 8–10×/hr minimum, 12–15×/hr optimal.
Training Implication
Undersized HVAC → heat accumulates during peak sessions → ↑ perceived exertion and injury risk independent of the workout itself.
Photo by 2H Media on Unsplash
Topic 05 — Environmental and Support Systems · 3 of 4

Sound — Cues Over Noise

What It Is
Acoustic design and sound system that keep volume under 90 decibels so coaching cues cut through.
How It Works
Sound-absorbing surfaces reduce echo off hard floors/walls; PA/music system zoned so cues aren't drowned out.
Training Implication
An athlete who can't hear a spotting cue over music is one step from a missed rep turning into an injury.
Photo by Kelly Sikkema on Unsplash
Topic 05 — Environmental and Support Systems · 4 of 4

Electrical Service — Powering the Floor

What It Is
Electrical capacity and outlet placement sufficient for every powered piece of equipment.
How It Works
GFCI-protected, properly grounded circuits sized for simultaneous treadmill/bike/screen load; outlets positioned to avoid cords crossing walkways.
Training Implication
A cord run across a lifting platform is a trip hazard waiting to happen — plan outlet placement into the layout, not after.
Topic 05 — Environmental and Support Systems

FactorFigure
Lighting — general gym areas20–30 fc (200–300 lux)
Lighting — resistance/group training areasup to 50 fc (500 lux)
LED color temperature4,000–5,000 K
Temperature — appropriate range68–78°F (20–26°C)
Temperature — optimal range68–74°F (20–23°C)

Topic 06 — Facility Amenities and Storage

Four Amenity Areas

Support spaces that don't hold a barbell but still shape how the facility functions day to day.

1
Walls & Mirrors
2
Hydration / Nutrition Spaces
3
Locker Rooms
4
Storage Spaces
Photo by sati on Unsplash
Topic 06 — Facility Amenities and Storage · 1 of 4

Walls & Mirrors — Feedback & Durability

What It Is
Mirrored walls for visual technique feedback; impact-resistant wall surfaces near free-weight zones.
How It Works
Mirrors set ≥6 in. (15 cm) from equipment and ≥20 in. (51 cm) off the floor — clearing an 18 in. (46 cm) plate if dropped.
Training Implication
Unprotected drywall behind a dumbbell rack is a repair bill waiting to happen — budget wall protection into the free-weight zone from day one.
Photo by Bluewater Sweden on Unsplash
Topic 06 — Facility Amenities and Storage · 2 of 4

Hydration & Nutrition Spaces

What It Is
Dedicated water access and a fueling area separate from the training floor.
How It Works
Water fountains/bottle-fill stations placed at multiple points; nutrition space kept away from equipment to avoid spills near electronics.
Training Implication
Placing hydration stations far from the floor reduces how often athletes actually use them mid-session — put water within reach.
Photo by Gildásio Filho on Unsplash
Topic 06 — Facility Amenities and Storage · 3 of 4

Locker Rooms — Sized for the Roster

What It Is
Change and storage space sized and separated appropriately by gender/team.
How It Works
Capacity planned for peak simultaneous team turnover, not just total roster size.
Training Implication
Undersized locker rooms create bottlenecks that push athletes late into sessions — plan for the busiest changeover window.
Topic 06 — Facility Amenities and Storage · 4 of 4

Storage Spaces — Off the Floor

What It Is
Dedicated square footage for bands, accessories, plates, and portable equipment — off the active training floor.
How It Works
Sized proportional to total equipment inventory; positioned near point of use to minimize retrieval time.
Training Implication
Equipment left on the floor because storage was underbuilt becomes a permanent trip hazard and a supervision blind spot.
Photo by Nolan Gorniak on Unsplash
Topic 06 — Facility Amenities and Storage

Numbers You Must Know

FactorFigure
Mirror clearance from equipment≥6 in (15 cm)
Mirror height off the floor≥20 in (51 cm)
Standard weight-plate diameter18 in (46 cm)

The 18 in. plate sets the real-world test for mirror height: a plate dropped near the mirror or leaned against the wall behind it still clears the glass by about 2 in. (5 cm).

Topic 07

Arranging Equipment
& Traffic Flow

Topic 07 — Arranging Equipment and Traffic Flow

Traffic Flow Principles

  • Sightlines Keep every zone visible from the supervision point → no equipment blocks the view
  • One-Way Flow Route athletes in a logical progression → warm-up → main lifts → conditioning, no backtracking
  • Buffer Zones ≥3 ft (0.9 m) between racks, barbells & dumbbells → stops a missed lift bleeding into the next zone
  • Intensity Gradient Arrange low-intensity areas near entry, high-intensity/max-effort areas deeper in the space
  • Clear Aisles 5–7 ft (1.5–2.1 m) wide main walkways; circuit machines 30–36 in. (76–91 cm) apart, Olympic bars ≥36 in. (91 cm) end to end
  • Grouping Cluster equipment by function → reduces cross-traffic between unrelated training zones
Topic 07 — Arranging Equipment and Traffic Flow

Clearances & Spacing

Photo by Ricardo Henri on Unsplash
Topic 07 — Arranging Equipment and Traffic Flow

Equipment Areas

  • Stretching Open mat space near entry → part of the intensity gradient's low end
  • Circuit Stations arranged in a loop → continuous flow between exercises
  • Free Weights ≥3 ft (0.9 m) clearance on all sides of racks/benches for spotting
  • Weightlifting ~8×8 ft (2.4×2.4 m) platform + cushion ≈ 130 ft² (12 m²) footprint per lifter; grouped away from through-traffic, tallest ceiling clearance
  • Testing Dedicated lane/space kept clear for standardized protocols
  • Aerobic 40–60 ft² (3.7–5.6 m²) per machine (treadmill largest at 53 ft²) — rows with sightlines to the floor
  • Track / Turf Linear space for sprint and agility work, clear of fixed equipment
  • Suspension Training Anchor point 7–9 ft (2.1–2.7 m) high, hardware rated ≥5,000 lb (22 kN) tensile, clear of walkways
Photo by sour moha on Unsplash

Topic 08

Maintaining & Cleaning
Surfaces & Equipment

Topic 08 — Maintaining and Cleaning Surfaces and Equipment

Building a Schedule

Daily / Weekly
Skin-contact mats/pads cleaned daily with germicidal cleaner; padding/vinyl daily or every other day.
Weekly: walls/ceilings/mirrors every 1–2 weeks minimum, cable/bolt visual check.
Monthly / Annual
Monthly: upholstery, cushioning, and moving-part inspection.
Annual: full equipment audit, flooring/turf condition assessment, HVAC servicing.
A cleaning schedule that only reacts to visible dirt misses the wear that actually causes equipment failure — inspect on a calendar, not on appearance.
Topic 08 — Maintaining and Cleaning Surfaces and Equipment

Photo by TruckRun on Unsplash
Topic 08 — Maintaining and Cleaning Surfaces and Equipment

Documentation & Inspection

Maintenance Logs
Every cleaning/inspection dated and signed → creates a defensible record.
Safety Inspections
Scheduled equipment safety checks, separate from routine cleaning → catch structural wear (frayed cables, cracked welds) early.
An undocumented inspection is legally equivalent to no inspection — the log is part of the safety system, not paperwork overhead.
